item.title: Teach the useful and the ornamental — but the useful first
item.content:
Franklin's curriculum design was governed by a triage of attention. Time is short and subjects are many, so he proposed that students "learn those Things that are likely to be most useful and most ornamental, Regard being had to the several Professions for which they are intended" (Proposals, 1749). Usefulness leads; ornament is welcome but secondary; and what counts as useful is tied to where the student is actually headed.

In practice this meant English taught well rather than years of rote Latin, writing and reckoning, history and practical science, learning by doing. The transferable method: when designing any program of learning, rank content by usefulness to the learner's real purpose, teach that first, and let polish follow. It is the same "judge by use" test he applied to ideas, aimed at a syllabus.

item.title: The virtue drill — build character one habit at a time, with a scoreboard
item.content:
Franklin concluded that resolving to be good does nothing; old habits have to be broken and new ones drilled. So he refused to attack all thirteen of his virtues at once. He worked one at a time until it became habitual, then moved to the next, and sequenced them deliberately so each made the next easier — Temperance first for a clear head, then Silence, then Order. He tracked daily failures as black marks in a ruled little book, turning self-improvement into a measurable process with feedback rather than a vow.

The judgment underneath: behaviour is built by drill and data, the way a gardener weeds one bed at a time. Franklin wrote that he judged it best "not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once" (Autobiography). The transferable technique: pick one habit, make it a daily yes/no you can score, master it before adding the next.

item.title: Franklin's writing voice — plain, concrete, ironic, built to be quoted
item.content:
How Franklin wrote, drawn from across the public-domain corpus. Plainness first: short Anglo-Saxon words, concrete images over abstractions, a printer's ear for rhythm. He prefers the homely metaphor that sticks — rust on a key, a leak in a ship, a cake diminished at the edges — to any high-flown generality.

Irony is his default setting. He argues by understatement and inversion, often saying the opposite of what he means and trusting the reader to catch it ("a great Empire, like a great Cake, is most easily diminished at the Edges"). He hides behind personas (Poor Richard, Father Abraham, Silence Dogood, Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim) so he can be blunter, funnier, or more devastating than he could in his own name.

In argument he is deliberately tentative — "I conceive," "it appears to me," never "certainly" — leaving the reader room to agree. He compresses wisdom into balanced, memorable maxims engineered for repetition. And he turns the joke on himself as readily as on others, which is what keeps the whole voice warm rather than preachy. To write as Franklin: be plain, be concrete, be wry, understate, and end on a line worth quoting.

item.title: Wealth is a means to independence, never an end in itself
item.content:
For all his counsel on getting and saving, Franklin's real interest was never accumulation. It was independence — being beholden to no creditor, ashamed before no man, master of one's own time. Money matters because poverty strips away spirit and even virtue: "It is hard for an empty bag to stand upright" (The Way to Wealth). A person without means struggles to stand upright morally and socially, not only financially.

This subordinates the whole economic programme to a human end. Diligence and thrift are duties and a path to dignity, not mere acquisitiveness — which is why he could close his most famous sermon on money by handing the matter over to Providence and a blessing on industry. The point of the bag being full is that you can finally stand.

item.title: The daily scheme — bookend the day with two questions
item.content:
Franklin ran his day on a fixed scheme, and bookended it with two questions that turned a schedule into a moral practice. The morning question, set as he planned the day, was "What good shall I do this day?" The evening question, set as he reviewed it, was "What good have I done to-day?" (Autobiography). Between them sat blocks for work, meals, reading, and — explicitly — "examination of the day."

The structure is simple and portable: an intention in the morning, an honest accounting at night, with the day's labour in between. It pairs naturally with the virtue-drill (the evening review is where you mark the day's faults) and with his belief that the best service to God is doing good to others — the questions literally ask, each day, what good. The transferable template: open with "what good shall I do," close with "what good have I done," and let the gap between the two pull your conduct upward.

1. TEMPERANCE — "Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation."
2. SILENCE — "Speak not but what may benefit others or yourself; avoid trifling conversation."
3. ORDER — "Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time."
4. RESOLUTION — "Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve."
5. FRUGALITY — "Make no expense but to do good to others or yourself; i.e., waste nothing."
6. INDUSTRY — "Lose no time; be always employed in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions."
7. SINCERITY — "Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly, and, if you speak, speak accordingly."
8. JUSTICE — "Wrong none by doing injuries or omitting the benefits that are your duty."
9. MODERATION — "Avoid extremes; forbear resenting injuries so much as you think they deserve."
10. CLEANLINESS — "Tolerate no uncleanliness in body, clothes, or habitation."
11. TRANQUILLITY — "Be not disturbed

judge.why: Item A establishes the general principle: morality is grounded in consequences (actual harm/benefit) rather than authority/commandment. Item B is the specific, concrete instantiation of that principle—Franklin's 13 virtues operationalize this consequentialist ethic through practical precepts designed to produce measurable behavioral results. Each virtue's definition reflects the consequence-based logic: 'eat not to dullness' (health consequence), 'speak not but what may benefit' (utility consequence), etc. B exemplifies how A's abstract ethical foundation becomes a working system. Clear general→specific direction.

item.title: Right and wrong are grounded in consequences, not authority
item.content:
Franklin deliberately kept the distinguishing tenets of every religious sect out of his project of moral perfection, so it could serve people of any faith. The reason was a clear ethical foundation: "vicious actions are not hurtful because they are forbidden, but forbidden because they are hurtful" (Autobiography). Morality, for him, rests on the actual harm or good actions do to human beings — not on commandment or custom.

This grounds virtue in observable consequences rather than divine or social fiat, which is why he could treat ethics as a practical engineering problem with means and methods, not merely a list of prohibitions. It connects his religion (conduct over doctrine), his economics (vices as self-harm), and his whole habit of testing things by their effects.

item.title: Source — The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
item.content:
Franklin's memoir, written 1771–1790, the primary source for the self-mastery, persuasion, and civic-building regions: the 13 virtues and the virtue drill, the "errata" habit, the Socratic-to-tentative shift, the Junto, the subscription library and institution template, the appearance of industry, and his pragmatic religion.

Public domain. Caution noted during this build: the common Project Gutenberg plain-text editions (#148, #20203) are truncated in Part One and omit the virtues, Junto, and library; a complete edition (e.g. ushistory.org's) is needed for the most important material.

item.title: Region: Self-mastery — character as something you engineer
item.content:
Franklin treated his own character as a project to be built, not a fate to be accepted. The throughline of this region: improvement is mechanical and iterative — find the defect, name it, drill the correction, measure progress. He attacked virtues one at a time, tracked daily faults in a ruled book, and kept the practice even when the ideal stayed out of reach because the striving itself made him better.

What connects here: the virtue drill, the "errata" habit of treating life-mistakes like printing errors to be corrected, the speckled-axe acceptance of partial success, self-knowledge through humour (the Gout dialogue), and the conviction that virtue is grounded in human consequences rather than authority. Tagged "self-mastery".

item.title: The portable maxim — a vivid personal rule beats an abstract principle
item.content:
Franklin didn't moralise in the abstract; he distilled a lesson into a portable phrase he could say to himself at the moment of temptation. From a childhood memory of overpaying for a toy whistle, he built a whole theory of human folly — but the operative part was the self-mocking line: "I said to myself, Don't give too much for the whistle; and I saved my money" (The Whistle, 1779).

It worked precisely because it was concrete, tied to a remembered sting, and short enough to surface when needed. He understood that maxims govern conduct only when they're memorable enough to fire at the point of decision — an abstract principle sits in a book; a vivid rule shows up in your head as you reach for your wallet. The transferable move: compress hard-won lessons into a phrase you can actually hear yourself say in the moment.

fragment.text:
Franklin ran his day on a fixed scheme, and bookended it with two questions that turned a schedule into a moral practice. The morning question, set as he planned the day, was "What good shall I do this day?" The evening question, set as he reviewed it, was "What good have I done to-day?" (Autobiography). Between them sat blocks for work, meals, reading, and — explicitly — "examination of the day."

The structure is simple and portable: an intention in the morning, an honest accounting at night, with the day's labour in between. It pairs naturally with the virtue-drill (the evening review is where you mark the day's faults) and with his belief that the best service to God is doing good to others — the questions literally ask, each day, what good. The transferable template: open with "what good shall I do," close with "what good have I done," and let the gap between the two pull your conduct upward.

item.title: The virtue drill — build character one habit at a time, with a scoreboard
item.content:
Franklin concluded that resolving to be good does nothing; old habits have to be broken and new ones drilled. So he refused to attack all thirteen of his virtues at once. He worked one at a time until it became habitual, then moved to the next, and sequenced them deliberately so each made the next easier — Temperance first for a clear head, then Silence, then Order. He tracked daily failures as black marks in a ruled little book, turning self-improvement into a measurable process with feedback rather than a vow.

The judgment underneath: behaviour is built by drill and data, the way a gardener weeds one bed at a time. Franklin wrote that he judged it best "not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once" (Autobiography). The transferable technique: pick one habit, make it a daily yes/no you can score, master it before adding the next.

item.title: The Junto — engineer a group so it thinks better than its members
item.content:
Franklin's club was not a debating society but a disciplined instrument for mutual improvement. Queries were circulated the week before so members read up and spoke "to the purpose," and the rules forbade the flat contradiction and disputatiousness that wreck conversation — even fining anyone too positive in their assertions. He saw this structure as the thing that made it, in his estimate, the best school of philosophy and politics in the province, and what made it last for decades.

He noted the queries, "read the week preceding their discussion, put us upon reading with attention" (Autobiography). The judgment: good thinking is a social, designed process — set the right questions in advance, police the manners, and a group becomes smarter than any one head in it.

fragment.text:
The concrete operating rules behind the Junto method. Two design choices did most of the work. First, manners were policed: "all expressions of positiveness in opinions, or direct contradiction, were after some time made contraband, and prohibited under small pecuniary penalties" (Autobiography) — dogmatism and flat contradiction were literally fined out of the room. Second, preparation was forced: "our queries, which were read the week preceding their discussion, put us upon reading with attention upon the several subjects, that we might speak more to the purpose" (Autobiography).

The standing queries themselves asked each member what they had read, observed, or encountered that the group could learn from, what citizens were thriving or failing and why, and how members might help one another. The transferable template for a thinking group: circulate the questions in advance so people arrive prepared, and ban the disputatious manner so disagreement stays productive. Structure plus civility, not brilliance, is what makes a group smart.

Item B zooms into the specific mechanics of how the Junto actually functioned—the concrete rules (fining dogmatism, pre-circulating queries) that made it work as a 'group-thinking machine.' This is a genuine general->specific relationship: A describes the strategic role and pattern the Junto played in Franklin's larger civic project; B provides the operational details that instantiate A's claim about the Junto being an 'engineered group-thinking machine.' B is not a sibling theme but the mechanisms underneath A's assertion.

item.title: Region: Civic & institutional building — scale private benefit into public good
item.content:
Franklin built the public world the way he built everything: prove a thing small among friends, formalise it with rules and a funding mechanism, then let a good template propagate itself. The Junto was his prototype — a designed instrument for mutual improvement — and the subscription library, fire company, watch, hospital, and academy all grew outward from that same pattern.

What connects here: the Junto as an engineered group-thinking machine (questions circulated in advance, manners policed); the institution template (small proof → articles → subscription → imitation across provinces); the no-credit launch that disarms envy; and his lifelong conviction that joint strength beats fractious independence. Tagged "civic-building". Overlaps with statecraft on union, and with persuasion on the no-credit move.

item.title: On alliances — bind a partner by interest, not by sentiment
item.content:
Franklin secured the French alliance of 1778 not by appealing to friendship but by making France see that helping America served France's own interest against Britain. The American victory at Saratoga (1777) supplied the proof that the cause was viable; the Treaties of Alliance and of Amity and Commerce followed in February 1778. He understood that a partnership grounded in aligned interest is durable, where one grounded in goodwill alone is not — a view he had put bluntly years before: "Bargaining has neither friends nor relations" (Poor Richard, 1736).

The stance is clear-eyed, not cynical. He kept faith scrupulously once allied, because reliability was itself in America's interest and reputation was capital. But the foundation he sought was structural: find where the other party's advantage genuinely overlaps with yours, build the deal there, and the commitment holds because it pays both sides to keep it.

fragment.text:
Franklin's conviction that union beats fracture was not a late-life idea; he argued it concretely in 1754, decades before the Constitution. As a Pennsylvania delegate to the Albany Congress he authored the Albany Plan of Union, a scheme for a single colonial government — rejected, in the end, by both the colonial assemblies and the Crown. His diagnosis of the danger was sharp: the French were emboldened by "the present disunited State of the British Colonies, and the extreme Difficulty of bringing so many different Governments and Assemblies to agree," while the enemy had "the very great Advantage of being under one Direction, with one Council, and one Purse" (Pennsylvania Gazette, 9 May 1754).

That editorial ran beneath his "JOIN, or DIE" woodcut — a snake cut into colonial segments, the first political cartoon in an American paper. The position is pure Franklin statecraft: scattered parts are weak precisely because they cannot agree quickly, and the remedy is a single shared structure. It is the same argument he would make at the Convention, here in its first and bluntest form.

judge.why: Item A states a general principle (union/collective strength beats separation/weakness), while Item B provides a specific historical instance where Franklin applied this exact principle — the 1754 Albany Plan proposing one colonial council and one purse to counter French advantage. The passage explicitly identifies the Albany Plan as a concrete manifestation of Franklin's lifelong conviction. The direction is clear: A is the overarching principle, B is its instantiation in a particular policy proposal. This is not two siblings sharing a theme; B directly exemplifies the logic articulated in A.

item.title: Union over fracture — joint strength beats separate weakness
item.content:
Across his career Franklin returned to the danger of separation among the states, and the conviction that collective strength beats fractious independence. At the Convention he warned that disunion would leave the states "on the point of separation, only to meet hereafter for the purpose of cutting one another's throats" (1787), and that their councils would otherwise be "confounded like those of the Builders of Babel." His instinct was always that joint wisdom and joint strength, despite the local interests and prejudices that joint deliberation drags in, beat the alternative of weakness apart.

This is the conviction beneath his lifelong institution-building and his famous calls for union: a whole deliberately assembled from imperfect parts is stronger than the parts left to themselves. He was willing to pay the costs of cooperation — slower decisions, diluted preferences — because the alternative was worse.

item.title: Region: Statecraft & union — humility as the glue of collective action
item.content:
Franklin's mature politics rests on a single move: doubt your own infallibility so a fractious body can act as one. He judged that no assembly of fallible, interested men could produce perfection, so the test of a constitution was not whether it was flawless but whether anything better was actually attainable — and he sacrificed his private objections to the public good, keeping them quiet so as not to weaken confidence in the new government.

What connects here: intellectual humility as the precondition for union; compromise as a deliberate, civic act of self-restraint; the insight that perceived unanimity is itself a source of governing power; argument by inversion as his political weapon (the satires); and union over fracture as a recurring conviction. Tagged "statecraft".

item.title: Argument by inversion — advocate the folly to expose it
item.content:
Franklin's sharpest political weapon was irony that argued the opposite of what he meant. Instead of refuting British colonial policy directly, he wrote "Rules by Which a Great Empire May Be Reduced to a Small One" (1773), donning the mask of a cynical adviser instructing ministers on how to lose an empire — each "rule" a mirror of a real grievance, and the joke being that Britain was already following them. His opener set the tone: "a great Empire, like a great Cake, is most easily diminished at the Edges."

In the companion "Edict by the King of Prussia," he flipped the perspective the other way, making Britons the victims: a fictional Prussian king claims ancient sovereignty over Britain and imposes the very restrictions Parliament levied on America — built from real British statutes, so readers' outrage was outrage at their own laws. The transferable method: when direct argument bounces off, dramatise the absurd version of your opponent's position until it indicts itself.

item.content:
Franklin made intellectual humility the practical glue of collective action. Long experience, he said, had repeatedly forced him to revise opinions he once held as certain, so "the older I grow, the more apt I am to doubt my own judgment, and to pay more respect to the judgment of others" (Convention speech, 1787). Certainty isolates; doubt, honestly held, makes room for others and for revision when experience teaches better. item.title: On alliances — bind a partner by interest, not by sentiment
item.content:
Franklin secured the French alliance of 1778 not by appealing to friendship but by making France see that helping America served France's own interest against Britain. The American victory at Saratoga (1777) supplied the proof that the cause was viable; the Treaties of Alliance and of Amity and Commerce followed in February 1778. He understood that a partnership grounded in aligned interest is durable, where one grounded in goodwill alone is not — a view he had put bluntly years before: "Bargaining has neither friends nor relations" (Poor Richard, 1736).

The stance is clear-eyed, not cynical. He kept faith scrupulously once allied, because reliability was itself in America's interest and reputation was capital. But the foundation he sought was structural: find where the other party's advantage genuinely overlaps with yours, build the deal there, and the commitment holds because it pays both sides to keep it.

item.title: The Vergennes letter — secure the deal, then repair the ally
item.content:
During the 1782–83 peace, the American commissioners (Franklin, Jay, Adams) negotiated preliminary terms with Britain somewhat separately, without keeping the French foreign minister Vergennes fully informed. Vergennes objected, and the alliance was suddenly at risk just as the war was being won. Franklin's response (letter of 17 December 1782) is a small masterpiece of damage control: he acknowledged the lapse gracefully, did not grovel, and reframed the quarrel as exactly what the enemy wanted — "The English, I just now learn, flatter themselves they have already divided us. I hope this little Misunderstanding will therefore be kept a perfect Secret."

The maneuver: he had already locked in the essential terms with Britain, then turned to mend the relationship with the ally — and did it by appealing to their shared interest in not handing Britain a victory. The transferable method: when you have had to act unilaterally, secure the substance first, then repair the relationship by pointing both parties at their common adversary rather than at each other.

item.content:
Across his career Franklin returned to the danger of separation among the states, and the conviction that collective strength beats fractious independence. At the Convention he warned that disunion would leave the states "on the point of separation, only to meet hereafter for the purpose of cutting one another's throats" (1787), and that their councils would otherwise be "confounded like those of the Builders of Babel." This is the conviction beneath his lifelong institution-building and his famous calls for union: a whole deliberately assembled from imperfect parts is stronger than the parts left to themselves. He was willing to pay the costs of cooperation — slower decisions, diluted preferences — because the alternative was worse.

item.title: Soft power — be liked, and let popularity do the negotiating
item.content:
Franklin's most original diplomatic move was to make himself an emblem. Rather than appear as a powdered courtier, he played the plain natural philosopher from the New World — a simple fur cap, plain dress, spectacles — and let French society fall in love with the image. His face was reproduced on medallions, prints, busts, and snuffboxes until, as he wrote his daughter, the copies "have made your father's face as well known as that of the moon" (letter to Sarah Bache, 1779). His witty French "bagatelles" — The Whistle, The Ephemera, the Gout dialogue — circulated in the salons as part of the same charm.

The reasoning underneath: in a court where America had little leverage, affection was leverage. A beloved envoy is hard to refuse, and a popular cause attracts allies on its own. The transferable method: when you are the weaker party, invest in being genuinely liked and in a clear, attractive public identity — goodwill opens doors that pressure cannot.

item.content:
Reflecting at the close of the American Revolution, with the Treaty of Paris settled, Franklin distilled a lifetime's view of conflict into a single balanced line. It is the statesman's version of his economics — count the true cost — applied to the most expensive thing nations do.

item.title: Franklin's writing voice — plain, concrete, ironic, built to be quoted
item.content:
How Franklin wrote, drawn from across the public-domain corpus. Plainness first: short Anglo-Saxon words, concrete images over abstractions, a printer's ear for rhythm. He prefers the homely metaphor that sticks — rust on a key, a leak in a ship, a cake diminished at the edges — to any high-flown generality.

Irony is his default setting. He argues by understatement and inversion, often saying the opposite of what he means and trusting the reader to catch it ("a great Empire, like a great Cake, is most easily diminished at the Edges"). He hides behind personas (Poor Richard, Father Abraham, Silence Dogood, Sidi Mehemet Ibrahim) so he can be blunter, funnier, or more devastating than he could in his own name.

In argument he is deliberately tentative — "I conceive," "it appears to me," never "certainly" — leaving the reader room to agree. He compresses wisdom into balanced, memorable maxims engineered for repetition. And he turns the joke on himself as readily as on others, which is what keeps the whole voice warm rather than preachy. To write as Franklin: be plain, be concrete, be wry, understate, and end on a line worth quoting.

item.title: Soft power — be liked, and let popularity do the negotiating
item.content:
Franklin's most original diplomatic move was to make himself an emblem. Rather than appear as a powdered courtier, he played the plain natural philosopher from the New World — a simple fur cap, plain dress, spectacles — and let French society fall in love with the image. His face was reproduced on medallions, prints, busts, and snuffboxes until, as he wrote his daughter, the copies "have made your father's face as well known as that of the moon" (letter to Sarah Bache, 1779). His witty French "bagatelles" — The Whistle, The Ephemera, the Gout dialogue — circulated in the salons as part of the same charm.

The reasoning underneath: in a court where America had little leverage, affection was leverage. A beloved envoy is hard to refuse, and a popular cause attracts allies on its own. The transferable method: when you are the weaker party, invest in being genuinely liked and in a clear, attractive public identity — goodwill opens doors that pressure cannot.

item.title: The Vergennes letter — secure the deal, then repair the ally
item.content:
During the 1782–83 peace, the American commissioners (Franklin, Jay, Adams) negotiated preliminary terms with Britain somewhat separately, without keeping the French foreign minister Vergennes fully informed. Vergennes objected, and the alliance was suddenly at risk just as the war was being won. Franklin's response (letter of 17 December 1782) is a small masterpiece of damage control: he acknowledged the lapse gracefully, did not grovel, and reframed the quarrel as exactly what the enemy wanted — "The English, I just now learn, flatter themselves they have already divided us. I hope this little Misunderstanding will therefore be kept a perfect Secret."

The maneuver: he had already locked in the essential terms with Britain, then turned to mend the relationship with the ally — and did it by appealing to their shared interest in not handing Britain a victory. The transferable method: when you have had to act unilaterally, secure the substance first, then repair the relationship by pointing both parties at their common adversary rather than at each other.

item.title: On alliances — bind a partner by interest, not by sentiment
item.content:
Franklin secured the French alliance of 1778 not by appealing to friendship but by making France see that helping America served France's own interest against Britain. The American victory at Saratoga (1777) supplied the proof that the cause was viable; the Treaties of Alliance and of Amity and Commerce followed in February 1778. He understood that a partnership grounded in aligned interest is durable, where one grounded in goodwill alone is not — a view he had put bluntly years before: "Bargaining has neither friends nor relations" (Poor Richard, 1736).

The stance is clear-eyed, not cynical. He kept faith scrupulously once allied, because reliability was itself in America's interest and reputation was capital. But the foundation he sought was structural: find where the other party's advantage genuinely overlaps with yours, build the deal there, and the commitment holds because it pays both sides to keep it.

item.title: Region: Diplomacy & negotiation — patience, image, and the long game
item.content:
Franklin spent nearly nine years in France (1776–1785) as America's envoy, and his diplomacy is a distinct mode of his thinking — slower, softer, and more theatrical than his other work. He did not win the French alliance by argument; he won it by being patient, by being liked, and by aligning France's interests with America's so the decision became France's own. The same temperament carried him through the 1783 peace.

What connects here: soft power (cultivating personal popularity and a deliberate public image as instruments of state); patience as leverage, letting situations ripen rather than forcing them; binding allies through interest rather than sentiment; the delicate management of a strained ally during the peace (the Vergennes letter); and the shaping of America's image abroad as a land of work and opportunity. Tagged "diplomacy". Overlaps with persuasion (image, indirection) and statecraft (alliance, peace, union).
